newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT--Dlr upside tied to lasting U.S. hike hope.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT--Dlr upside tied to lasting U.S. hike hope.

text.p: Analysts see more upside in store for the dollar for as long as strong U.S. economic data keep expectations of a near-term U.S. rate hike alive.
The dollar broke through good resistance levels -- in particular against the yen -- on Friday, leaving the field wide open for fresh gains next week.
In a shortened Friday session ahead of a three-day Labor Day weekend, the dollar ended at 1.4804/11 marks and at 108.90/00 yen, clearly above strong support levels at 1.4750 marks and 108.50/55 yen.
U.S. markets will be closed on Monday for Labor Day.

Analysts said that, in a repeat of Thursday's session, the dollar set higher highs and higher lows than on the prior day -- a bullish signal. Also, the break of 108.75 yen was important, they added, because it indicates a breakout on the upside with 109.40 as the next goal.
Technicians saw initial resistance at 1.4820 marks and 109.20 yen, preluding for a more ambitious attack on 1.4840 marks and 109.40 yen.
MCM CurrencyWatch analyst Kevin Harris cautioned that volatility on the European crosses could unleash a renewed appetite for the safe-haven German mark and Swiss franc.

"Through the (September) budget season, European currencies will get a lot of interest. The word is already out Italy's budget won't include any social program cut, while, in France, social spending this year is worse than previously thought and next year should not be better," Harris said.
Amid such budget worries, mark/Paris brushed on Thursday the key psychological level at 3.4305 -- the top of the old European Rate Mechanism band.
Harris said the European crosses will "look shaky for as long as the budget season is under way," which may, at times, indirectly hurt dollar/mark and dollar/Swiss.

Meanwhile, the dollar outlook is dependent on the market's perception of the U.S. monetary policy outlook, mainly next week when the key economic reports of the month are released and may sway the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.
Harris was more upbeat about dollar/yen because "if you have an extended period of steady rates (in Japan), the carry trade is safe since you'll never find yourself facing rising financial costs."
"Confidence the Bank of Japan won't raise rates is always positive for the dollar block, mainly the high-yielders such as Canada," Harris concluded. -- Isabelle Clary, 212-859-1666
